## Overview {#main-content}

How much more likely is a bill to clear committee with each additional cosponsor? How much does a year of schooling raise the chance that someone turns out to vote? And is either answer the same for every case, or does it depend on which cases you have in mind? A logistic regression coefficient cannot settle any of these. It gives the direction of a relationship and its size on the log-odds scale, and its hypothesis test says whether the relationship is distinguishable from zero. Neither says how many percentage points the predicted probability moves. That has to be computed, and it is not one number --- the same difference in a predictor is worth a great deal for some cases and almost nothing for others.

This tutorial shows how to answer the size question with prediction plots, which trace the predicted probability across a predictor's whole range rather than at one or two points. It builds on Tutorial 20, where you estimated the two models and computed predicted probabilities for particular counties and states, and on Tutorial 17, which introduced prediction plots for linear models. What is new is deciding which cases a plot should describe, because here that decision sets the size you report. You will do that with `plot_model()` from the [sjPlot]{.package-name} package, where `terms` names the predictors the plot varies and `condition` changes the value a predictor is held at when the default will not do.

In this tutorial you will learn:

* Why a logistic regression coefficient cannot say how much a predictor moves the probability of an outcome, and why the honest answer depends on which cases you are describing
* How to choose the values the other predictors are held at, rather than accepting `plot_model()`'s defaults --- setting them with `condition` where the substance calls for it --- defend that choice, and state it in the caption so a reader knows which cases the claim covers
* How to report a relationship across the range the cases in your data actually occupy, rather than across values no case has, which is what `plot_model()`'s bracket notation is for
* How to put the same relationship in two contexts in one figure, by naming values inside `terms`, so a reader can see whether a finding holds in both
* How to read a categorical predictor's predicted probabilities, and tell a difference concentrated in one category from one spread across all of them
* How to separate what a prediction plot establishes about the size of a relationship from what only a coefficient test establishes about whether it could be zero --- including why two curves that never cross are a claim the model is making rather than a feature of the picture

                   gov_f + econ_poverty2022,
                 family = "binomial", data = statesPolicy)

# Reads the terms = argument actually passed to plot_model(), so a grader can
# compare it with what the exercise asked for. A text search cannot: the string
# "electoral_f" is present in terms = c("electoral_f", "quota_f") as well.
# Bracket notation is normalized, so "x[all]" and "x [all]" are the same term,
# and so are "x [0.70,0.86]" and "x [0.70, 0.86]".
qpa_norm_terms <- function(x) {
  x <- trimws(x)
  x <- gsub("\\s*\\[\\s*", " [", x)
  x <- gsub("\\s*\\]", "]", x)
  x <- gsub("\\s*,\\s*", ", ", x)
  x <- gsub("\\s+", " ", x)
  # Canonicalize numbers inside brackets so .7, 0.7 and 0.70 all compare equal.
  # Non-numeric contents such as [all] and [meansd] are left untouched.
  vapply(x, function(s) {
    br <- regmatches(s, regexpr("\\[[^]]*\\]", s))
    if (!length(br)) return(s)
    parts <- trimws(strsplit(substr(br, 2L, nchar(br) - 1L), ",")[[1]])
    nums  <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(parts))
    if (anyNA(nums)) return(s)
    sub("\\[[^]]*\\]", paste0("[", paste(as.character(nums), collapse = ", "), "]"), s)
  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}

qpa_plot_terms <- function(user_code) {
  code  <- paste(user_code, collapse = "\n")
  exprs <- tryCatch(as.list(parse(text = code)), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(exprs)) return(NULL)
  out <- NULL
  walk <- function(x) {
    if (!is.call(x)) return(invisible(NULL))
    if (identical(deparse(x[[1]])[1], "plot_model") && is.null(out)) {
      args <- as.list(x)[-1]
      nm   <- names(args)
      if (!is.null(nm) && any(nm == "terms"))
        out <<- tryCatch(qpa_norm_terms(as.character(eval(args[[which(nm == "terms")[1]]]))),
                         error = function(e) NULL)
    }
    for (part in as.list(x)[-1]) walk(part)
  }
  for (e in exprs) walk(e)
  out
}

qpa_terms_msg <- function(got, want) {
  w <- qpa_norm_terms(want)
  as_arg <- function(v)
    if (length(v) == 1) paste0("`terms = \"", v, "\"`")
    else paste0("`terms = c(\"", paste(v, collapse = "\", \""), "\")`")
  if (length(got) > length(w))
    return(paste0("Your call passes ", as_arg(got), ". Every variable named in `terms` varies in the plot: a second name draws a separate series for it rather than holding it constant, and the caption you wrote states that it was held. Use ", as_arg(want), "."))
  if (length(got) == length(w) && setequal(got, w))
    return(paste0("The right variables in the wrong order. The first name in `terms` goes on the x-axis and the second draws one series per category. Use ", as_arg(want), "."))
  if (!identical(gsub("\\s*\\[[^]]*\\]", "", got), gsub("\\s*\\[[^]]*\\]", "", w)))
    return(paste0("Your call passes ", as_arg(got), ". Use ", as_arg(want), "."))
  paste0("The variables are right but the bracket notation is not. Brackets after a variable name tell `plot_model()` which values to draw that variable at. Use ", as_arg(want), ".")
}
```

## Choosing the Cases Your Plot Describes

A fitted logistic regression can produce a predicted probability for any combination of predictor values you supply. A prediction plot therefore describes particular cases, not the data in general. One predictor varies along the x-axis, while the others are held at specified values or, for a comparison, allowed to take two or more values. Consider the turnout question from the overview: in a model of turnout with schooling, income and age, holding income and age at their averages describes a voter of average income and age, while holding income near the bottom of its range describes a voter with low income. The plot's interpretation depends on which values you choose.

You made similar choices in Tutorial 17, but they mattered less for interpreting the size of a relationship. In an additive linear regression, changing the held values shifts the predicted line up or down without changing its slope. The same difference in a predictor is associated with the same difference in the outcome regardless of the other predictors' values.

**Logistic regression is different.** The S-curve is steep in the middle and nearly flat at both ends. Changing the values held constant changes where predictions fall on that curve. The same difference in a predictor might correspond to only a few percentage points for one kind of case and tens of percentage points for another. Both answers come from the same fitted model, with the same coefficients and hypothesis tests. Neither is necessarily wrong; they describe different cases. Choosing which cases matter is therefore part of interpreting the model, not merely a plotting decision.

How should you choose? Start with the research question and the cases relevant to it. A useful default is to hold other predictors at their typical values and describe a difference across the interquartile range of the predictor you vary, which covers the middle half of the observed cases. Sometimes the question calls for the full observed range instead, when what you want to know is how much a relationship can be worth at all rather than what it is worth among ordinary cases; say which span you used either way. The `summary()` function reports central tendencies and quartiles to help make these decisions. When particular groups matter, examining the distributions within those groups may also be useful, although we do not do that here.

Holding predictors at their overall averages creates a standardized comparison case, not necessarily a typical member of a particular group. An Urban county with otherwise average county characteristics is not necessarily typical of Urban counties, which tend to be more educated and less white than counties overall. Whatever values you select, describe them in words and report them in the plot caption. A comparison of counties with different racial compositions tells readers more than a comparison of curves labeled 0.70 and 0.86.

As in Tutorials 15 through 20, we use *predictor*, *predicts* and *effect* in their statistical sense; none of them by itself implies causation. A prediction plot shows what the fitted model predicts for particular cases, not what would happen if a county or state's characteristics were changed.

## How Do County Characteristics Relate to the Predicted Probability of a Trump Majority?

Trump took a majority of the two-party vote in 2,622 of the nation's 3,112 counties while losing the national popular vote. The 490 counties he did not carry were a different kind of place: their college graduation rate averaged 0.29 against 0.19 elsewhere, and their proportion white 0.69 against 0.89.

Two arguments about 2016 account for that pattern differently, one economic and one demographic, and Tutorial 20 tested expectations from both. The demographic argument rests on those two differences:

::: {.hypothesis}

In a comparison of counties, those with lower college graduation rates will be more likely to give a majority of their two-party vote to Donald Trump than those with higher college graduation rates.

:::

::: {.hypothesis}

In a comparison of counties, those with higher proportions of white residents will be more likely to give a majority of their two-party vote to Donald Trump than those with lower proportions of white residents.

:::

It found support for both, and for the economic argument only in part: working-age mortality risk was associated with a Trump majority while wage growth was not distinguishable from zero. What the coefficients left unsettled is what those two relationships amount to: how many percentage points of predicted probability separate a county where few adults hold degrees from one where many do, whether that figure is the same in counties of different racial composition, and in which counties a Trump majority was the more likely outcome at all. Those are the questions this example works out, first for education and racial composition and then for the other characteristics in the model.

The model you estimated in Tutorial 20 predicts whether a county gave Trump a majority of the two-party vote (**TrumpMajority**) from the percent change in average weekly wages (**wage_growth**), the proportion of adults 25 and older holding a bachelor's degree, on a 0-to-1 scale (**prop_college_grad**), the proportion of residents who are white (**prop_white**), the percentage risk of dying between 25 and 45 (**mortality_risk_25_45**), and whether the county is Urban, Intermediate or Rural (**rural_cat**). The variables describe counties as of 2016, apart from wage growth, which measures change over the twelve months ending in the third quarter of that year. The outcome and rurality have no missing values; education, racial composition and mortality risk are each missing for one county and wage growth for two, so the model is estimated on 3,109 of the 3,112 counties.

The model output below reproduces the coefficients for reference. Compare the z values as you read: education and racial composition are estimated far more sharply than wage growth, mortality risk or rurality, so the two characteristics the hypotheses name are also the two this model speaks to with the most confidence.

```{r model-trump-recall, echo=TRUE, comment=NA}
summary(model_trump)
```

The coefficients say which relationships the model found. What they cannot say is which counties to describe, and that decision needs the predictors themselves.

```{r predictor-summary, echo=TRUE, comment=NA}
summary(counties[c("prop_college_grad", "prop_white", "mortality_risk_25_45", "wage_growth")])
```

Two things in that output matter for what follows. Half of all counties have college graduation rates between 0.14 and 0.25, the first and third quartiles, and that is the span across which to report an educational difference. And the proportion white has a median of 0.93 against a mean of 0.86, so holding it at its mean already describes a county more racially diverse than most.

### How Is Education Related to the Probability a County Cast a Majority for Trump?

There is no one number that says what education is worth, because in logistic regression a predicted probability depends on the value of every explanatory variable in the model. What can be answered is narrower: for a county that is Urban and otherwise average across all counties, how does education change the predicted probability of a Trump majority? Which kind of county to ask about follows from the research question and what you want to show.

Here we ask it of a county that is Urban and otherwise average across all counties. Urban is worth asking about because Urban counties are where the outcome varied: Trump took a majority of the two-party vote in 74% of them, against 89% of Intermediate counties and 93% of Rural ones. These are `plot_model()`'s defaults, so no extra argument is needed to produce them --- and, as the last section said, they give a standardized comparison rather than a typical Urban county.

Two things in the code below are worth noting before you run it. `library(sjPlot)` appears because this is the tutorial's first use of `plot_model()`, and `colors = cb_colors` passes the colorblind-safe palette from Tutorial 4, which the setup defines and every plot in this tutorial uses.

**Run and observe 1: The default prediction plot, and the message it produces**

Run the code below and look at two things: the message that appears above the plot, and the shape of the line.
```{r exercise-predplot-college-default, exercise=TRUE, exercise.cap="Run and observe 1", fig.alt="Predicted probability of a Trump majority against the proportion of adults with a college degree. The horizontal axis runs from 0 to 1. The line consists of three points joined by two straight segments meeting at a corner near the middle, falling from close to 100 percent at the left to near 0 at the right."}
library(sjPlot)  # first use in this tutorial; it stays loaded from here on
plot_model(model_trump,
           type       = "pred",
           terms      = "prop_college_grad",
           colors     = cb_colors,
           title      = "Predicted Trump Majority Across County Education Rates",
           axis.title = c("Proportion of Adults with a College Degree",
                          "Predicted Probability of Trump Majority")) +
  labs(caption = "Predictions are for Urban counties with average wage growth, mortality risk, and proportion white (0.862).")
```

That line is not an S-curve. It is two straight segments meeting at a corner, and the message above the plot explains why. `plot_model()` does not compute a prediction at every value a variable takes. It picks a small set of round, evenly spaced values, computes predictions there, and joins them. The message calls this prettifying. For **prop_college_grad** it chose three values --- 0, 0.5 and 1 --- so the plot has three points and two straight lines between them. The S-shape the model actually implies is invisible at that resolution.

There is a second problem, and it is the more serious one. No county in the data has a college graduation rate above about 0.80, and none is at 0. Two of the three points fall outside the range of the data entirely, so the plot is showing you predictions for counties that do not exist.

The message also tells you the fix. Adding `[all]` inside the quoted variable name --- `terms = "prop_college_grad [all]"` --- tells `plot_model()` to use the values the variable actually takes instead of a handful of round numbers. The curve is then smooth, and it covers only the range the counties actually span. Treat the message as a prompt to add the brackets whenever it appears, in this tutorial and in your own work.

**Practice 2: Draw the curve at the graduation rates counties actually have**

The call is repeated below. Add the bracket notation to `terms =` so the plot is drawn at every observed value, and change nothing else. The `condition` argument is not needed: the defaults are the held values described above.

Two hints are available. Click "Submit Answer" to check your work.
```{r exercise-predplot-college, exercise=TRUE, exercise.cap="Practice 2", fig.alt="The same relationship drawn as a smooth curve. The horizontal axis runs from about 0.03 to about 0.80. The curve is close to 100 percent at the left and declines very gradually at first: about 97 percent at a graduation rate of 0.14 and about 89 percent at 0.25. It then falls steeply through the middle of the range, passing 50 percent at about 0.42, and approaches 0 at the right. A shaded band follows it."}
plot_model(model_trump,
           type       = "pred",
           terms      = "prop_college_grad",
           colors     = cb_colors,
           title      = "Predicted Trump Majority Across County Education Rates",
           axis.title = c("Proportion of Adults with a College Degree",
                          "Predicted Probability of Trump Majority")) +
  labs(caption = "Predictions are for Urban counties with average wage growth, mortality risk, and proportion white (0.862).")
```

```

```{r exercise-predplot-college-check}
grade_this({
  code             <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
  code_no_comments <- gsub('("(?:\\\\.|[^"\\\\])*")|#[^\r\n]*', "\\1", code, perl = TRUE)
  if (grepl("=\\s*[TF](?![A-Za-z._0-9])", code_no_comments, perl = TRUE)) {
    fail("Write `TRUE` and `FALSE` in full. R accepts `T` and `F` as shorthand, but these tutorials do not: `TRUE` and `FALSE` are reserved words and always mean what you expect, while `T` and `F` are ordinary object names that other code can overwrite --- after which an argument set to `T` or `F` quietly means something else. Replace them with `TRUE` and `FALSE` and submit again.")
  }

  if (!grepl("plot_model\\s*\\(", code_no_comments))
    fail("Use `plot_model()` to produce the prediction plot.")
  if (!grepl("plot_model\\s*\\(\\s*model_trump\\b", code_no_comments))
    fail("Pass **model_trump** as the model object.")
  if (!grepl("Predicted Trump Majority Across County Education Rates", code_no_comments, fixed = TRUE))
    fail("Use the prescribed title: \"Predicted Trump Majority Across County Education Rates\".")
  if (!grepl("type\\s*=\\s*['\"]pred['\"]", code_no_comments))
    fail("Set `type = \"pred\"` to produce a prediction plot.")
  if (!grepl("colors\\s*=\\s*cb_colors", code_no_comments))
    fail("Set `colors = cb_colors` so the plot uses the colorblind-safe palette.")
  tm <- qpa_plot_terms(.user_code)
  if (is.null(tm))
    fail("Name the argument that decides which variable goes on the x-axis.")
  if (!identical(tm, "prop_college_grad [all]"))
    fail(qpa_terms_msg(tm, "prop_college_grad [all]"))
  if (!grepl("axis\\.title\\s*=", code_no_comments))
    fail("Include the `axis.title =` argument with the prescribed labels.")
  if (!grepl("Proportion of Adults with a College Degree", code_no_comments, fixed = TRUE))
    fail("Use the prescribed x-axis label: \"Proportion of Adults with a College Degree\".")
  if (!grepl("labs\\s*\\(", code_no_comments))
    fail("Add a labs(`caption = \"...\"`) layer stating the held values.")
  if (!grepl("Predictions are for Urban counties", code_no_comments, fixed = TRUE))
    fail("Use the prescribed caption.")

  # The checks above find the required pieces somewhere in the submission; this
  # one establishes they belong to the plot actually produced.
  if (!inherits(.result, "ggplot"))
    fail("Your last line should produce the plot itself, so `plot_model()` is what prints.")
  bl <- tryCatch(ggplot2::ggplot_build(.result), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(bl))
    fail("The plot could not be built. Check that every argument sits inside the `plot_model()` call.")
  lb <- .result$labels
  chk <- function(field, want, what) {
    got <- lb[[field]]
    if (is.null(got) || !identical(gsub("\\s+", " ", as.character(got)),
                                   gsub("\\s+", " ", want)))
      fail(paste0("The plot's ", what, " is not the prescribed one --- check it is set inside this plot rather than elsewhere in your code."))
  }
  chk("x", "Proportion of Adults with a College Degree", "x-axis label")
  chk("y", "Predicted Probability of Trump Majority", "y-axis label")

  pass("Well done. The message is gone, the curve is drawn at every observed value, and the x-axis now covers only the range counties actually occupy. The shape of the curve, the caption and the confidence band are now all describing the same set of counties.")
})
```


The college graduation rate runs from about 0.03 to about 0.80 across counties, and half of them fall between 0.14 and 0.25. With the curve drawn at the rates counties actually have, you can read what it says about them.

**Practice 3: Identify what the model predicts for most counties**

```{r quiz-college-read, echo=FALSE}
question("These predictions are for a county that is Urban and otherwise average across all counties. Half of all counties have college graduation rates between 0.14 and 0.25. What does the curve show about counties like that?",
  correct = "Right. Nearly every county of this description falls where the curve is high and flat.",
  answer("A Trump majority was the more likely outcome for nearly all of them, and education separates them by only about 8 percentage points, from about 97% at 0.14 to about 89% at 0.25",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "The curve is nearly flat across that range. It stays above 50% until a graduation rate of about 0.42, which only about 3% of counties exceed."),
  answer("A Trump majority was the more likely outcome for nearly all of them, and education is associated with almost no difference anywhere across its observed range",
         message = "Not anywhere. From 0.30 to 0.40 the predicted probability falls about 24 points. It is the middle half of counties that sits on the flat part of the curve."),
  answer("A Trump majority was the more likely outcome for about half of them, because the predicted probability passes 50% inside that range of graduation rates",
         message = "The 50% line is a probability, not a count of counties. The curve is above 89% across that whole range and does not reach 50% until about 0.42."),
  answer("A Trump majority was the more likely outcome only for the least educated of them, because the predicted probability is already below 50% by a graduation rate of 0.25",
         message = "At 0.25 the predicted probability is still about 89%. It does not reach 50% until a graduation rate of about 0.42."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  try_again = "Read the curve at 0.14 and at 0.25, then find where it passes 50%."
)
```
The steep part of the curve, where education is associated with large differences in predicted probability, describes the small minority of counties with the highest graduation rates rather than the counties the data mostly contain. Whether the same holds in every kind of county is the next question.

The confidence band is widest there too, spanning about 19 percentage points at a graduation rate of 0.42 against two to five points across the middle half of counties. In Tutorial 17's linear plots the band was narrowest in the middle of the data and widened toward both ends; here it does the opposite, because near a probability of 0 or 1 the curve flattens and the same uncertainty is worth far fewer percentage points.

### How Much Does Education Separate Counties of Different Racial Composition?

Across the middle half of counties, education separated the average county's predictions by only about 8 percentage points. That figure describes one kind of county, and the next question is whether it describes others. Changing one held value gives a second kind: the proportion white drops from its mean of 0.86 to 0.70. That is more racially diverse than most counties, and 446 of them are at least that diverse. Everything else stays where it was --- Urban, with average wage growth and mortality risk --- so the two curves differ in one respect only.

How do we draw both curves in one figure? Brackets are not only for `[all]`. Naming specific values inside them --- `"prop_white [0.70, 0.86]"` --- tells `plot_model()` to draw one curve for each value instead of holding the variable at its mean. Named second in `terms`, that variable becomes the grouping variable, so the plot draws two education curves. Brackets take literal numbers rather than `mean()`, so 0.86 stands in for the mean of 0.8619. This is the first plot here with more than one line on it, which is why the palette matters and why it needs a legend title: without one, `plot_model()` labels the legend with the variable name, and a reader sees **prop_white** rather than what it measures.

grade_this({
  code             <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
  code_no_comments <- gsub('("(?:\\\\.|[^"\\\\])*")|#[^\r\n]*', "\\1", code, perl = TRUE)
  if (grepl("=\\s*[TF](?![A-Za-z._0-9])", code_no_comments, perl = TRUE)) {
    fail("Write `TRUE` and `FALSE` in full. R accepts `T` and `F` as shorthand, but these tutorials do not: `TRUE` and `FALSE` are reserved words and always mean what you expect, while `T` and `F` are ordinary object names that other code can overwrite --- after which an argument set to `T` or `F` quietly means something else. Replace them with `TRUE` and `FALSE` and submit again.")
  }

  if (!grepl("plot_model\\s*\\(", code_no_comments))
    fail("Use `plot_model()` to produce the prediction plot.")
  if (!grepl("colors\\s*=\\s*cb_colors", code_no_comments))

  tm <- qpa_plot_terms(.user_code)
  if (is.null(tm))

  want_tm <- qpa_norm_terms(c("prop_college_grad [all]", "prop_white [0.70, 0.86]"))
  # Either order of the two values draws the same pair of curves.
  if (!identical(tm, want_tm) &&
      !identical(tm, qpa_norm_terms(c("prop_college_grad [all]", "prop_white [0.86, 0.70]"))))
    fail(qpa_terms_msg(tm, want_tm))
  if (!grepl("plot_model\\s*\\(\\s*model_trump\\b", code_no_comments))
    fail("Pass **model_trump** as the model object.")
  if (!grepl("Predicted Trump Majority by Education, at Two Racial Compositions", code_no_comments, fixed = TRUE))
    fail("Use the prescribed title: \"Predicted Trump Majority by Education, at Two Racial Compositions\".")

  if (!grepl("Proportion White", code_no_comments, fixed = TRUE))

  if (!grepl("labs\\s*\\(", code_no_comments))

  if (!grepl("Predictions are for Urban counties with average wage growth and mortality risk.", code_no_comments, fixed = TRUE))
    fail("Use the prescribed caption: \"Predictions are for Urban counties with average wage growth and mortality risk.\". Racial composition is no longer held constant, so it does not belong in the caption --- it is in the legend.")

  # The checks above find the required pieces somewhere in the submission; this
  # one establishes they belong to the plot actually produced.
  if (!inherits(.result, "ggplot"))
    fail("Your last line should produce the plot itself, so `plot_model()` is what prints.")
  bl <- tryCatch(ggplot2::ggplot_build(.result), error = function(e) NULL)

Both curves come from the same fitted model. Compare what the middle half of counties looks like on each.



**Practice 5: Compare how much education separates each kind of county**

```{r quiz-college-condition, echo=FALSE}
question("Half of all counties have college graduation rates between 0.14 and 0.25. Across that range, how much does the predicted probability of a Trump majority differ in each of the two kinds of county?",
  correct = "Right. Same coefficient, same span of education, three times the difference.",
  answer("About 8 percentage points in the average county and about 24 in the more diverse one, because that range lies on the flat part of one curve and inside the steep middle of the other",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "One education coefficient produces both. Across that range the average county's curve is nearly flat near the top while the more diverse county's is passing through its steep middle, so a Trump majority stops being the likely outcome at 0.29 there rather than 0.42."),
  answer("About 8 percentage points in the average county and about 24 in the more diverse one, so the model estimates a larger education coefficient where counties are more diverse",
         message = "The two figures are right. The model is additive, though, and estimates one education coefficient applied at every proportion white."),
  answer("About 24 percentage points in the average county and about 8 in the more diverse one, because the average county's curve is the steeper of the two across that range",
         message = "The other way round. Across that range the average county's curve is nearly flat while the more diverse county's falls steeply."),
  answer("About 8 percentage points in both, since the model applies one education coefficient whatever the proportion white",
         message = "One coefficient does apply throughout. It is worth about 8 points where the curve is flat and about 24 where it is steep, and the two curves are in different places across this range."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  try_again = "Compare how steeply each curve falls between 0.14 and 0.25."
)
```

::: {.important-note}

**The two curves have the same shape.** This model is additive: it estimates one education coefficient and applies it whatever the proportion white. Lowering the proportion white shifts the whole curve to the left --- about 0.14 in graduation rate --- without making it steeper or flatter. Nothing about the relationship differs between the two kinds of county. What differs is which part of the curve the counties you are describing occupy, and near a probability of 0 or 1 the curve flattens, so the same span of education is worth far fewer percentage points there. That is [S-curve compression]{.important-text}, and it is why one coefficient produced about 8 points in one case and about 24 in the other.

:::

### Are the Two Kinds of County More Alike Where Distress Is Greatest?

Tutorial 20 tested a second argument about 2016 alongside the demographic one. Counties where working-age adults faced higher mortality risk were taken to be registering economic and social distress, and that distress was expected to move them toward Trump. The relationship held. The deaths-of-despair literature behind the argument developed around predominantly white communities, which makes the more racially diverse counties the interesting comparison.

The plot below keeps both kinds of county from the last one and puts mortality risk on the x-axis, with the college graduation rate held at its average. Mortality risk varies across its full observed range rather than its middle half, because the question is how much difference distress can be associated with at all rather than what it is worth among ordinary counties.

One mortality coefficient, applied in both kinds of county, is associated with about 15 percentage points in the one already near certainty and about 46 in the other. Something further follows from that: where distress is greatest, racial composition is associated with almost no difference in the predicted probability, because both kinds of county sit near the top of the curve there. Racial composition separates counties sharply where distress is low and barely at all where it is high, and one additive model produced both.

### Do Predicted Probabilities Rise Steadily from Urban to Rural Counties?

Rurality is the last of the characteristics this example describes, and Tutorial 20 found a Rural county more likely to give Trump a majority than an Urban one. Whether that difference accumulates from Urban through Intermediate to Rural, or sits between Rural and the other two, is a question about predicted probabilities rather than coefficients. Answering it means putting rurality itself on the x-axis, which also stops holding it at Urban --- the reference category used for every prediction so far in this example. The other four predictors are held at their means, which makes these three predictions a comparison of rurality alone.

**rural_cat** is a three-category variable. When `terms` names a categorical variable, `plot_model()` plots the predicted probability for each category with a confidence interval rather than a continuous curve --- there is no meaningful range to sweep across for a categorical variable, only discrete levels to compare. Each predicted probability is for one rurality category at the held values stated in the caption.

### What We Learned About Education, Mortality Risk, and Trump Support

Both demographic composition hypotheses receive support in the county-level analysis, and Tutorial 20's coefficients established both directions. What the coefficients could not report is the size, and the plots in this example report it four times for differently described counties. The answers do not agree, and that disagreement is the finding rather than a complication of it.

For a county that is Urban and otherwise average across all counties, education is associated with about 8 percentage points across the middle half of counties, and a Trump majority remains the more likely outcome until the graduation rate passes about 0.42 --- a rate only about 3% of counties exceed. Lower the proportion white to 0.70 and nothing about the fitted model changes, but the same educational span is worth about 24 points and a Trump majority stops being the more likely outcome at about 0.29. One education coefficient produced all of it. What differed was which part of the curve the counties being described occupy.

Mortality risk shows the same thing in a different form. Across its full observed range the predicted probability rises about 15 percentage points for the average county and about 46 for the more diverse one, and the distance between the two closes from about 33 points to about 3. Where distress is greatest the model predicts a Trump majority for both kinds of county alike, because both predictions lie near the top of the curve.

Rurality adds a smaller difference, and it is where the default the other three plots relied on gets examined. For counties at the means of the other four predictors, Urban and Intermediate are predicted near 92-93% and Rural near 95%, so only Rural sits above the other two. The finding to carry out of this example is the one all four plots show: a single fitted model, and an answer no more specific than the counties you have described.

A complete interpretation of the college graduation prediction plot reads like this:

::: {.research-example}

*As the proportion of adults with college degrees increases, the predicted probability of a Trump majority falls, following an S-curve from near certainty at low graduation rates to near zero at high ones. These predictions are for a county that is Urban and otherwise average across all counties; for such a county a Trump majority remains the more likely outcome until the graduation rate passes about 0.42, a rate only about 3% of counties exceed. Across the middle half of counties, 0.14 to 0.25, the predicted probability falls only about 8 percentage points, because that span lies on the flat upper part of the curve. Reported across the fuller span from 0.10 to 0.45 the drop is about 55 points, from about 98% to about 43%, but only about 4% of counties fall below 0.10 and about 3% above 0.45, so that figure describes few real places. The curve for a much more racially diverse county, at a proportion white of 0.70, lies lower throughout and passes 50% at about 0.29, and across the same middle half the drop there is about 24 points rather than 8. The confidence band is narrowest at both ends of the range, within a few percentage points, and widest through the middle, about 19 points at a graduation rate of 0.42, which is the same compression at work on the uncertainty. This pattern is consistent with the demographic composition argument: after controlling for economic distress and geography, the model implies a substantial difference in the predicted probability of a Trump majority across county educational attainment, and a larger one in the more racially diverse counties the argument concerns.*

:::


## How Much Does the Predicted Probability of an Emissions Cap Differ Across States?

States differ sharply in whether they have a greenhouse gas emissions cap. Tutorial 20 asked whether that difference tracks the ideological composition of a state's population, its governor's party, or its economic circumstances.

The model you estimated in Tutorial 20 predicts whether a state has a greenhouse gas emissions cap (**policy_ghgcap2024**) from the percentage of residents identifying as conservative (**ideology_conservative2024**), the governor's party, with Democrat as the reference category (**gov_f**), and the state poverty rate (**econ_poverty2022**). The variables come from different years: the emissions cap and the governor's party as of 2024, conservative identification from the 2024 PRRI American Values Atlas, and the poverty rate from 2022. Only conservative identification has a missing value, for the District of Columbia, so the model is estimated on the 50 states.

Tutorial 20 found conservative identification negatively associated with having a cap, after accounting for governor party and the poverty rate. How much does the predicted probability differ between a relatively liberal state and a conservative one, and at what level of conservative identification does a cap become unlikely in states with different poverty rates?

The model output below reproduces the coefficients for reference. Pay particular attention to the ideology coefficient and its significance before producing any plots.

```{r model-ghg-recall, echo=TRUE, comment=NA}
summary(model_ghg)
```

As in the county example, the predictors themselves decide which states are worth describing.

```{r ghg-predictor-summary, echo=TRUE, comment=NA}
summary(statesPolicy[c("ideology_conservative2024", "econ_poverty2022")])
```

Half of all states have conservative identification between 31% and 41%, so that is the span across which to report an ideology difference. Poverty rates run from 7.2% to 19.1%, and the two values used later in this example, 8% and 18%, sit outside the middle half deliberately: the question there is what the ideology relationship looks like in states at either end of the poverty distribution.

### How Is Conservative Identification Related to the Probability a State Has a Cap?

This question has no general answer either: the predicted probability depends on the governor's party and the poverty rate as well. The plot below answers it for a Democrat-governed state at the average poverty rate of 12.4%, and a Republican governor or a different poverty rate would give a different answer. The two plots that follow make exactly those changes.

States with more conservative public opinion are less likely to have emissions caps, even after controlling for governor party and poverty rate. This relationship is significant and central to the hypothesis, which makes it the one to visualize first. The prediction plot shows the full S-curve across the observed range of conservative identification (14% to 50%), making visible what the coefficient of -0.296 could not communicate on its own. Use `plot_model()` to examine the predicted probability of an emissions cap across that range, holding governor party at Democrat and the poverty rate at its mean.

Governor party is categorical, so `plot_model()` holds it at its reference category, Democrat, in the first two plots of this example --- 23 of the 50 states. That is a default rather than a choice, and the last two plots stop relying on it by naming governor party in `terms`, so both parties appear. `condition` is only needed when you want something other than the defaults, and `color` only when a second variable in `terms` produces separate curves. The caption is not optional: nowhere else does a reader learn which values the other predictors were given.

### Does the Poverty Rate Change Where a Cap Becomes Unlikely?

This plot changes one held value and nothing else: the governor's party stays at Democrat, the fitted model is the same one, and the poverty rate moves from its mean of 12.4% to 8% and to 18%. Observed poverty rates run from 7.2% to 19.1%, so 8% and 18% describe real states near either end of the distribution. The poverty rate has its own negative coefficient in this model, which Tutorial 20 could not distinguish from zero at the conventional threshold, p = .073. The fitted model still produces a predicted probability at any poverty rate you name.

One figure answers it. Naming both values in brackets --- `"econ_poverty2022 [8, 18]"` --- draws the ideology curve once for each, the same move you used for racial composition in the county model.

### Is the Party Gap in the Plot Evidence of a Party Difference?

This plot stops holding governor party at its Democrat reference category and puts both parties in the figure, and the poverty rate returns to its mean of 12.4%. A two-variable prediction plot puts **ideology_conservative2024** on the x-axis and produces separate S-curves for Democrat- and Republican-governed states. Because the model has no interaction between ideology and governor party, the curves will not cross: the model estimates one ideology coefficient and applies it in both kinds of state, with governor party moving a state's starting point rather than changing how ideology relates to the outcome. The gap between the curves may still narrow near the extremes, where S-curve compression leaves little room in either direction. That gap is what governor party is worth across the ideology range.

### Where Does the Party Gap Fall in a High-Poverty State?

It takes a named list, `condition = list(variable = value)`. Using it here asks the same question in a different setting: what do the two governor-party curves look like in a high-poverty state?

# and axis.title inside the same plot_model() call. It takes a
# named list pairing the poverty variable with the value the
# prompt gives. Everything else is unchanged except the caption
# text.
```

  if (length(unique(bl$data[[1]]$group)) != nlevels(statesPolicy$gov_f))

You now have the same two curves in two economic contexts. Compare them before answering.

**Practice 17: Compare the two governor-party plots**

```{r quiz-twovar-ghg-cond, echo=FALSE}
question("The two plots hold poverty at 12.4% and at 18%. What does the comparison show?",
  correct = "Right: the curves shift left, so the same party gap turns up at a different level of conservative identification.",
  answer("Both curves sit lower, and the widest party gap is about 32 points in both plots but falls at about 27% conservative identification in one and about 17% in the other",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "The governor-party coefficient has not changed, so the largest gap it can produce has not changed either. Raising poverty shifts both curves left, which moves where that gap falls."),
  answer("The party gap is smaller in the high-poverty plot --- about 3 points at 30% conservative identification against about 28 --- so governor party matters less in poor states",
         message = "At a fixed point that is what you see --- 28 points at 30% conservative identification in the first plot, 3 points in the second. But each plot's widest gap is about 32 points, because the log-odds governor party coefficient is the same in both."),
  answer("Both curves drop by the same number of percentage points at every level of conservative identification, since poverty enters the model additively",
         message = "That is what a linear model would do. Here the drop is 49 points at 20% conservative identification and about 15 points at 35%, because the same difference in log-odds produces different numbers of percentage points at different places on the curve."),
  answer("The curves are closer together at every level of conservative identification in the high-poverty plot, because the ideology coefficient is smaller there",
         message = "One model, one ideology coefficient, used in both plots. Nothing about the fitted model changed between them; only the value poverty was held at."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  try_again = "Find the widest gap between the two curves in each plot, and note where along the x-axis it falls."
)
```

### What We Learned About Ideology, Poverty, and Climate Policy

The ideology hypothesis holds, and the plots say what it is worth. The plots put the coefficient of -0.296 on the probability scale: across the middle half of states, from 31% to 41% conservative identification, the predicted probability of having a cap falls from about 39% to about 3% for a Democrat-governed state at the average poverty rate --- about 36 percentage points. A wider span gives a larger figure, and across 20% to 35% the drop is about 78 points, but only one state is as liberal as 20%.

The predicted probabilities differ sharply by poverty rate. A Democrat-governed state at 35% conservative identification has a predicted probability of about 67% when the poverty rate is 8% and about 16% at the average poverty rate, a difference of about 51 percentage points. The ideology coefficient is identical in both predictions; what differs is the poverty rate held constant, and Tutorial 20 could not distinguish the poverty coefficient from zero at the conventional threshold.

The two-variable plot puts the governor-party comparison across the whole ideology range. Republican-governed states sit below Democrat-governed ones throughout, and the fitted gap reaches about 32 points, but Tutorial 20 could not distinguish that coefficient from zero, p = .208. The curves never cross, because the log-odds ideology coefficient is the same in both kinds of state; governor party moves the starting point only. And the widest gap falls at about 27% conservative identification at average poverty and at about 17% in a high-poverty state. The largest party difference the model produces is about 32 points in both contexts, but at any particular level of conservative identification the predicted difference can be far larger at one poverty rate than at the other.

A complete interpretation of the ideology prediction plot reads like this:

::: {.research-example}

*The predicted probability of having a greenhouse gas cap drops steeply as conservative identification increases, following an S-curve from near certainty at the low end of the ideology range to near zero at the high end. Predictions hold governor party at Democrat and poverty rate at its mean (12.4%); the curve for a high-poverty state lies lower throughout, since the poverty rate has its own negative coefficient in the model, although Tutorial 20 could not distinguish that coefficient from zero at the conventional threshold. Across the middle half of states, from 31% to 41% conservative identification, the predicted probability falls from about 39% to about 3%, a drop of about 36 percentage points. Reported across the wider span from 20% to 35% the drop is about 78 points, but only one state is as liberal as 20%, so that figure describes a comparison almost no state could enter. In this plot, the confidence band is widest through much of the steep middle region. That width partly reflects compression near probabilities of 0 and 1, although it also depends on where the observations are concentrated and how precisely the model parameters are estimated. This pattern is strongly consistent with the hypothesis that ideology is associated with climate policy, and the prediction plot makes visible what the significant coefficient of -0.296 could not convey: across the steep middle of the range, the predicted difference is very large.*

:::


## Check Your Understanding

The two examples showed that held values decide which part of the S-curve a prediction plot displays, that the shape of the curve shows what the coefficient table cannot, and that reading such a plot means reading its caption as carefully as its line. The questions below ask you to apply these ideas to new scenarios without looking back at the examples.

**Apply 18: Defend a change in slope**

A researcher fits a logistic model of whether a city has adopted a climate action plan, using population density, median income, and the proportion of residents with a college degree. She produces two prediction plots with population density on the x-axis: one at the means of the other predictors, and one conditioned on a high median income. The curve in the second is noticeably steeper. A reviewer objects that one plot must be wrong, because changing what you hold constant can only move a line up or down, not change its shape.

```{r quiz-cyu-steepness, echo=FALSE}
question("Who is right, and why?",
  correct = "Right. Held values decide which part of the S-curve you are looking at.",
  answer("The researcher. Held values decide where on the S-curve the predictions fall, and the curve is steeper in the middle than at its ends",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "In a linear model the reviewer would be right: a held value shifts the line and leaves the slope alone. In a logistic model it relocates the predictions along the S-curve, which is steep in the middle and flat at both ends."),
  answer("The reviewer. Holding a variable at a different value shifts the entire curve vertically by that variable's coefficient, so the two curves must have the same shape",
         message = "That is right for linear regression. On the log-odds scale the shift is constant; on the probability scale it is not, because the conversion from log-odds to probability is not a straight line."),
  answer("The reviewer, because a prediction plot can only show one relationship at a time, so the two plots must have been produced from different models",
         message = "Both plots come from the same fitted model. `condition` changes the values the other predictors are held at when the predictions are computed, not the model they come from."),
  answer("The researcher, because conditioning on a high median income re-estimates the model using only high-income cities, which produces different coefficients and so a different slope",
         message = "Conditioning does not re-estimate anything. The model is fitted once, on all the data; the condition argument only chooses the values at which the fitted coefficients are evaluated when the predictions are computed. Every coefficient is the same in both plots."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  try_again = "Ask whether the two curves come from different coefficients, or from the same coefficients evaluated somewhere else on the curve."
)
```

**Apply 19: Interpret converging curves**

In an additive logistic model of whether a bill received a committee hearing, a researcher plots the number of cosponsors on the x-axis with separate curves for majority-party and minority-party sponsors. The curves are far apart at low cosponsor counts and nearly meet at high ones. They do not cross.

```{r quiz-cyu-converging, echo=FALSE}
question("What does the narrowing gap tell you about the relationship between sponsor party and the probability of a hearing?",
  correct = "Right. The log-odds difference is constant; what it is worth in percentage points is not.",
  answer("The difference in predicted probabilities narrows near the top of the S-curve, even though the estimated party difference in log-odds stays constant",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "On the log-odds scale the party difference is the same at every cosponsor count. Converting to probabilities compresses that constant difference into fewer percentage points as both curves approach 1."),
  answer("That the model estimates a smaller sponsor-party coefficient for heavily cosponsored bills, since the two curves nearly meet at high cosponsor counts",
         message = "The model estimates one sponsor-party coefficient and applies it at every cosponsor count. The predicted difference narrows near the top of the S-curve because both curves approach 1, not because the estimate changes."),
  answer("That the two curves were computed from separate models, one fitted to majority-party sponsors and one to minority-party sponsors",
         message = "One model, one party coefficient, both curves. The gap narrows because of where the predictions fall on the probability scale, not because anything was estimated twice."),
  answer("That sponsor party is not a significant predictor once the number of cosponsors is accounted for, since the curves end up in nearly the same place",
         message = "Significance is settled by the coefficient's test, not by how far apart two curves look at one end of the range. The curves are far apart through the middle, which is where the party coefficient is most visible on the probability scale."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  try_again = "Think about what a constant difference in log-odds looks like once it is converted to probabilities near the top of the scale."
)
```

**Apply 20: Identify what the band shows**

A prediction plot shows the probability that a country holds a competitive election as a function of GDP per capita, with a shaded band around the curve. The band is narrow at low GDP and much wider through the middle of the range.

```{r quiz-cyu-band-meaning, echo=FALSE}
question("What does the shaded band represent, and what does its changing width reflect?",
  correct = "Right. Uncertainty about the estimated probability, compressed near the bounds of the scale.",
  answer("Uncertainty in the estimated probability, whose width in percentage points shrinks near 0 and 1 because the probability scale is compressed there",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "The band answers how precisely the model locates the curve, given that the coefficients came from a sample. Its width in percentage points is not constant, because the same coefficient uncertainty spans fewer points near the bounds."),
  answer("The range within which the outcomes of individual countries fall, so it is narrow where nearly all countries share the same outcome",
         message = "The outcomes are 0 or 1, so no interval strictly between them could contain an individual outcome. The band describes the estimated probability, which is a property of the model."),
  answer("The spread of the observed data around the fitted curve, so it is wider where countries vary more in whether they hold competitive elections",
         message = "That describes residual scatter, which is not what is drawn here. The band comes from uncertainty in the estimated coefficients, and it would exist even if the model fitted the data perfectly."),
  answer("How well the model fits at each value, so a wide band means the model describes those countries poorly",
         message = "Band width is not a measure of fit. A model can fit badly and still produce a narrow band if its coefficients are precisely estimated, and compression near 0 and 1 narrows the band whatever the fit."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  try_again = "Ask what quantity the band is uncertain about --- the probability the model estimates, or the outcome of any particular country."
)
```

**Apply 21: Diagnose an incomplete interpretation**

A student writes the following interpretation of a prediction plot showing the relationship between a country's unemployment rate and the probability that the incumbent government loses re-election. Unemployment in the data ranges from about 2% to about 20%.

*"As the unemployment rate rises, the predicted probability that the incumbent loses increases. Each additional point of unemployment raises the predicted probability by about 4 percentage points. At an unemployment rate of 30%, defeat is essentially certain."*

```{r quiz-cyu-diagnose-logistic, echo=FALSE}
question("Which of the following best identifies what is wrong with this interpretation?",
  correct = "Right: a constant per-unit change, no held values, and a prediction beyond the data.",
  answer("It reports a constant change per unit, omits the held values, and reads a prediction outside the range of the data",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "Three faults. A logistic curve has no single per-unit change, so \"about 4 percentage points\" can be true somewhere but not everywhere; without the held values a reader cannot tell which part of the curve is described; and 30% lies beyond the observed range."),
  answer("Nothing is wrong --- the direction is right, the magnitude is specific, and the interpretation ends with a concrete prediction",
         message = "Specificity is not the same as accuracy. A single per-unit figure misdescribes a curve whose slope changes across its range, and the concrete prediction at the end is at a value no country in the data reaches."),
  answer("The only problem is the missing held values; stating what the other predictors were fixed at would complete the interpretation",
         message = "Adding the held values is necessary and not sufficient. The constant per-unit claim would still misdescribe the shape of the curve, and the prediction at 30% would still be an extrapolation past the data."),
  answer("The only problem is the causal implication --- rewriting the claim as an association rather than an effect would complete the interpretation",
         message = "The interpretation is already phrased as what the model predicts, so causal language is not the fault. The problems are the constant per-unit change, the missing held values, and the prediction beyond the observed range."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  try_again = "Check the claim about magnitude against the shape of an S-curve, and check the final prediction against the range the data cover."
)
```

## The Takeaways

Tutorial 17 introduced prediction plots for additive linear-regression models, where the values held for the other explanatory variables shift the predicted line up or down and leave its slope alone. Any defensible set of held values described different cases but reported the same size of relationship. In logistic regression the choice changes the size itself. The held values determine which part of the S-curve the plot shows, and so how many percentage points the relationship is worth across the range you report. The coefficient gives the direction and a size on the log-odds scale; the number of percentage points has to be read off a curve, and there is no single such number. The prediction plot is part of interpreting the model rather than an illustration of something already visible in the coefficients table.

::: {.qpa-infographic}
<table class="qpa-table">
  <caption>Describing Relationships by the Outcome's Level of Measurement</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th class="qpa-corner" scope="col"><span class="visually-hidden">Aspect of the relationship</span></th>
      <th scope="col">Interval Outcome</th>
      <th scope="col">Categorical Outcome with Two Categories</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">What the Model Fits</th>
      <td>A straight line through the conditional means of the outcome</td>
      <td>An S-curve for the probability that the outcome equals 1</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">What a Coefficient Means</th>
      <td>The expected difference in the outcome for a one-unit difference in the predictor, the same everywhere along the range</td>
      <td>The direction and size of the relationship on the log-odds scale, the same everywhere along the range --- not a number of percentage points</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">How You Report the Size</th>
      <td>The slope, or the predicted difference between two cases</td>
      <td>A predicted probability difference, which depends on the values the other predictors are given</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">What the Held Values Do</th>
      <td>Shift the line up or down; the slope is unchanged</td>
      <td>Decide where on the S-curve the comparison falls, so they change the size</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Visualization</th>
      <td>A prediction line, straight across the range</td>
      <td>A prediction curve, flattening as it approaches 0 and 1</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">R Functions</th>
      <td><code>lm()</code>, <code>predict()</code>, <code>plot_model(type = "pred")</code></td>
      <td><code>glm(family = "binomial")</code>, <code>predict(type = "response")</code>, <code>plot_model(type = "pred")</code></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
:::

**`plot_model()` from [sjPlot]{.package-name}.** The `plot_model()` function from the [sjPlot]{.package-name} package produces prediction plots from fitted models. For logistic regression, the key arguments are:

- `type = "pred"` to produce a prediction plot on the probability scale
- `terms =` to name the variable on the x-axis (a single string for a single-variable plot, or `c("x_variable", "group_variable")` for a two-variable plot)
- `axis.title =` to label the x-axis and y-axis, in that order
- `legend.title =` to title the legend, when a second variable in `terms` separates the curves
- `+ labs(caption = "...")` to add a caption describing the held values

When `terms =` names an interval variable, `plot_model()` produces a continuous S-curve. When `terms =` names a categorical variable, it produces a predicted probability with a confidence interval for each category --- there is no continuous range to sweep across for a categorical variable, only discrete levels to compare.

**Bracket notation.** When `terms =` names an interval variable, `plot_model()` computes predictions at a handful of round values rather than at every observed value, and prints a message saying so. Adding `[all]` inside the quotation marks --- `"variable_name [all]"` --- computes a prediction at the observed values of the variable, which both smooths the curve and confines it to the range the data actually cover. A categorical variable has only its categories, so it needs no bracket notation and produces no message.

**The `condition` argument.** The values the other explanatory variables are fixed at are the plot's [held values]{.important-text}. By default `plot_model()` uses their means (for interval variables) or their reference category (for categorical variables). The `condition` argument overrides those defaults: `condition = list(variable_name = value)` holds the named variable at the specified value while the x-axis variable varies. You can set multiple variables at once: `condition = list(variable1 = value1, variable2 = value2)`. The most useful condition values are *substantively meaningful* --- corresponding to real, recognizable cases rather than arbitrary numbers. When substantively justified values sit in different regions of the S-curve, comparing them shows how the same fitted relationship appears in different contexts. The caption is not a formality: it is essential information about what the plot is actually showing, and reading it carefully is part of applying the five-component framework.

**Reading non-crossing curves.** When `terms =` names two variables, `plot_model()` produces one curve per level of the grouping variable. In an additive logistic model --- one without an interaction term --- the same x-axis coefficient applies within every group, and the curves do not cross. The vertical gap between them is widest through the steep middle of the probability scale and narrows toward 0 and 1, which is [S-curve compression]{.important-text}. A narrowing gap is a fact about where the predictions fall, not evidence that the coefficient differs between groups.

**Reading the confidence band.** In Tutorial 17's linear plots the band was narrowest near the middle of the data and widened toward both ends of the range, because a prediction is least certain where there is least data. On the probability scale that pattern is reversed. The uncertainty in the estimated log-odds still grows as you move away from the data --- in the county model it is smallest where counties are thickest and largest at the top of the graduation range, where a single county sits --- but converting log-odds to probabilities compresses it near 0 and 1 exactly as it compresses the predicted differences. The band is therefore widest where the curve is steepest and narrow at both ends, even though the estimates at those ends are the least precise. A narrow band near 0 or 1 is not evidence that the model describes those cases well.

**The five-component framework.** Every prediction plot, regardless of what model produced it, can be read using the same five components introduced in Tutorial 17:

1. **The pattern** --- the direction and shape of the relationship as the x-axis variable increases
2. **The held values** --- what the other explanatory variables were set to, and what that means for how the result generalizes
3. **Specific predicted values** --- what the model predicts at substantively meaningful points along the x-axis
4. **The uncertainty** --- the width of the [confidence band]{.important-text} and whether it varies across the range
5. **The hypothesis connection** --- whether the pattern is consistent with the hypothesis that motivated the model, and what the plot adds beyond the significance test

In logistic regression the held values deserve particular attention. They determine which part of the S-curve the plot shows, and therefore both the pattern you describe and the predicted values you report.

This tutorial closes the regression sequence that began in Tutorial 15. What matters afterward is not a function but a habit: any claim about the size of a relationship in a logistic model rests on a choice of held values, and the claim is only as good as the defense of that choice and the caption that states it. In your own analysis that choice is yours to make and to justify.
